articles.title: âAttackers took bath, ate datesâ: Chilling details in Bangladesh Hindu family case
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city. Investigators said the suspects allegedly stayed at t.
articles.body: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city. Investigators said the suspects allegedly stayed at the house after the killings, bathed there, ate dates and cucumbers from the refrigerator and used yaba before fleeing, as per local media reports.The victims were identified as retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 23, and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty. Their bodies were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area at around 11.30pm on Saturday.According to Bangladeshâs Prothom Alo, Rangpur police commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud said two suspects, identified as Mugdha and Siddhartha, remained inside the house after the killings. Police said they left on Friday when the streets were relatively empty during Jummah prayers.Before leaving, the suspects allegedly opened cupboards and drawers and scattered clothes and other belongings around the house, apparently in an attempt to make the incident appear to be a robbery. Investigators also found items allegedly used for taking yaba on a table inside the house.Police said evidence was found suggesting that an attempt had been made to test a gold bangle using fire. Two mobile phones belonging to the victims had also allegedly been submerged in water mixed with detergent, possibly in an attempt to destroy evidence.The suspects were identified and detained based on these clues, Prothom Alo reported. Police said they confessed to the killings during questioning. Gold jewellery allegedly looted from the home was later recovered from an abandoned location indicated by the two detainees.Date pits found inside the house have been seized and sent for DNA testing, according to Prothom Alo.The bodies were found in different parts of the house. Subir Chowdhury, in-charge of Rangpur Metropolitan CID, said the mother and daughter were found on the staircase, Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof and Priyamâs body was found under a bed.âThe household belongings were found scattered and in disarray. For now, it appears to be a robbery. However, nothing can be confirmed until the investigation is completed,â he said.Sanatan Chakrabarty, deputy commissioner of Rangpur Metropolitan Police and head of the Detective Branch, said the victims were initially suspected to have been strangled. He said the killings may have taken place between midnight on Thursday and early Friday.The family had not been heard from since Thursday. Pritilataâs sister Puja Chakraborty told The Daily Star that all four phones had been switched off.âWe came to Daspara on Saturday night after finding their phones switched off. The main gate of the house was locked and all the lights inside were off. Police later arrived, broke the lock and entered the house, where they recovered the bodies,â she said.Police, CID and Detective Branch teams are jointly investigating the killings. AKM Nazmul Kader, officer-in-charge of Rangpur Kotwali police station, said preparations were under way to file a murder caseCatch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Frustration builds in US city struggling without power for 12 days
articles.summary: In the town of Gary, where a third of residents live in poverty, people say they have been living in "survival mode".
articles.body:
Nearly two weeks after a damaging storm struck her town in Indiana, Terry Dubois is one of tens of thousands of people still without power.

The 77-year-old has been relying on friends to bring her non-perishable food to eat.

Her son brought her a power bank so she can charge her phone and keep in touch with the outside world.

Thankfully, the summer heat hasn't been too punishing, Dubois says, meaning she has not missed her air conditioning too much.

"I've never seen a storm like that in my entire life. Never, never," she tells the BBC.

"It was like a sheer wall of wind," she recalls.

A wave of sudden, severe storms brought flooding and tornadoes to the US Midwest on 11 August, including to Chicago and Indiana, where seven people were killed.

The former industrial town of Gary, which runs along the southern shore of Lake Michigan, was hit particularly hard. Wind gusts peaked at 99mph (159km/h), according to the National Weather Service.

The worst of the storm only lasted five to 10 minutes, but the impacts are lingering 12 days later.

Power has been restored to more than 345,000 customers since the storm struck, but almost 30,000 were still without power as of Sunday morning, according to the area's electrical company Northern Indiana Public Service Company (Nipsco).

In the first few days after the storm, petrol stations, supermarkets and pharmacies were without power, leaving people to survive on what they had.

As the outage stretched into a second week, global food charity World Central Kitchen arrived to help people without access to food.

Power outages are not out of the ordinary for this part of the US. But outages that last more than a week are uncommon.

Once home to the world's largest steel mill, the former industrial heartland of Gary has felt the outage on many fronts. One third of its roughly 70,000 residents live in poverty, according to US Census data.

As well as dealing with storm-damaged properties, residents of the former industrial town have struggled to source food and maintain good hygiene.

There have also been reports of people unable to refrigerate medication and a wheelchair user crawling down their stairs in the absence of working lifts.

At night, some roads have been "pitch black" without working street lights, Gary resident Kyle Allen tells the BBC.

Allen has faced shorter power outages before, but this experience has been different as he has started caring for his 95-year-old father.

As a result, he bought a generator which has been sustaining him and his father since the power failed.

Shatiya Hardin, meanwhile, said the situation has been "absolutely horrible".

"At night we're sweating, we're irritable, we have children to look out for, elderly people who need electricity for oxygen tanks," she told the BBC's US partner CBS.

"It's not OK for us to continually be in survival mode."

Amid mounting frustration, local residents have launched a class-action lawsuit, accusing the utility company Nipsco of failing to manage the trees that brought down the power lines in the storm.

In the lawsuit, resident Jack Tipold said he was in the middle of dental surgery when the power failed.

He said he was forced to abandon the procedure and was discharged without adequate pain medication.

"I had all my teeth removed and no medication for 48 hours. Let me tell you something, it was a struggle," he told CBS.

Nipsco has denied wrongdoing and said it would "vigorously" defend itself in court.

Faith leaders alarmed by the ongoing outage held a news conference on Saturday outside a local church.

"We come together today with one voice, asking those who have the power... to release the resources to our brothers and our sisters, our mothers and our fathers, because 12 days is long enough," he said, according to the Indianapolis Star.

Nipsco said on Sunday that it was restoring power to everyone as soon as possible and estimated Gary would have its electricity restored by Wednesday.

"We recognise how frustrating and difficult it is to be without power for an extended period," the company said in a statement.

Indiana's Governor Mike Braun said on Sunday that there was "no excuse for these delays".

He has requested a quicker major disaster declaration from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema), which would unlock further help.

With climate change making extreme weather more severe and frequent, such power outages are likely to become a more common problem.

In the meantime, Braun has pushed Nipsco to bring in more crews to get those without power back online, telling the firm: "Put every available resource into the field. Get creative."

articles.title: 1975 homicide of 27-year-old Norris ‘Snookie’ Evans remains unsolved | Dateline
articles.summary: Norris “Snookie” Evans, a 27-year-old mother of four, was found stabbed to death in her Rochester, New York, home in 1975. Rochester police say the case remains open.
articles.body: In 2021, Tamara Sinclair posted on a local Rochester, New York, Facebook page called “Remember when?” Among its usual posts where members reminisce over long-closed diners and share faded photographs from days gone by, Tamara’s post stood out. She asked if anyone remembered the 1975 murder of her mother, 27-year-old Norris “Snookie” Evans. “My sister was on Facebook and then she just threw that out there,” Daryl Evans told Dateline. A crime author came across Tamara’s post and offered to help her access the Rochester Police Department’s case documents. Tamara says what she read forever altered her understanding of her mother’s death. A life cut short Dateline obtained the same report from the Rochester Police Department. The initial entry states that at 11:24 p.m. on May 23, 1975, Rochester Police dispatch received a phone call reporting “family trouble” at a home on Kron Street in the city’s 19th Ward. According to the report, Officer Paul Camping was dispatched to the scene, where he knocked repeatedly on the front door to no response. Finding the house dark and quiet, he left. The report notes that an hour later, at 12:33 a.m., police received another call: this time from Snookie’s husband, Lewis Evans. Officer Camping returned to the scene and found Lewis “standing outside in an incoherent condition.” He told the responding officer he had just returned home from work at Rochester Products, a local manufacturing company, when he discovered his wife. Snookie was found dead in the living room, “lying face down with her ankles tied together with a white cloth,” according to the police report. The report also notes that a kitchen knife and a cast-iron frying pan were strewn on the floor, and the living room TV was on. Although the home appeared ransacked, there were no signs of forced entry. Lewis told police at the time that $1,100 in cash was missing from a metal box in the living room. The medical examiner’s office determined Snookie had multiple stab wounds and noted she had been nearly decapitated. The estimated time of death was placed between 11:30 p.m. and 12:30 a.m. Tamara was just 3 months old when her mother was killed. Daryl was only 2. Their half brothers on their father’s side were 4 and 6. They were all found inside the home, unharmed. Although Tamara and Daryl have no memories of their mother, the descriptions they’ve heard over the years are consistent: a sweet, devoted parent. Growing up, Snookie was close to her sister, Ellen Evans. “We walked to school together, eat lunch together. We just did everything together,” Ellen told Dateline. “She was the one who kept me grounded. She was the calm.” Gina Alves, married to Snookie and Ellen’s cousin at the time, fondly remembers her friendship with Snookie. “Norris is just so sweet. I really loved her,” Gina told Dateline. “Through her pregnancy, with — what they call him, Tiger — Daryl, he was the cutest baby, and then she got pregnant with her daughter. She was just so excited, you know, ‘Oh, I got a girl! I got a girl!’” Gina says Snookie called her the night she died and asked if she wanted to play cards. “I’ll never forget that I was watching [The] Andy Griffith [Show] and she said, ‘Well, why don’t you guys come over?’” Gina said, choking up. She didn’t end up going. “So then, you know, that happened to her, and I always wonder, maybe if we would’ve went over there, maybe that wouldn’t have happened to her.” Ellen told Dateline she remembers the exact moment their father told her what happened to Snookie. “I slapped him. I slapped him so hard and told him, ‘You’re lying. You’re lying,’” she said. The investigation The Rochester Police Department launched an investigation into Snookie’s killing that would span years, chasing lead after lead. According to their report, Rochester police first looked into those with histories of violent burglaries in the area. They investigated at least 10 people who fit the description, checking fingerprints, administering polygraph exams and checking alibis without making an arrest. Ellen Evans told Dateline the family had its suspicions. She had introduced Snookie to Lewis Evans, the brother of Ellen’s estranged husband. “At first they were happy together,” she said. But as the relationship evolved, Ellen says it became clear to her that Snookie had grown scared of Lewis. “And all of a sudden, he was jealous, and he didn’t want us to hang out together.” Police also spoke with Ellen and Snookie’s cousin Ronald Purdue, who said he received a call from Snookie the morning of her death. “The victim stated to him that she was very depressed and she wanted to get away from her husband, as she was no longer in love with him,” the police report states. “She went on to say that because she was afraid of her husband she was afraid to leave.” Two days after his interview, Ronald called the Rochester Police Department and said he had additional information. A sergeant was dispatched to his residence to interview Ronald and his wife. According to the police report, Ronald said Snookie’s grandmother had asked young Daryl if he knew who hurt his mommy, to which the toddler responded, “Daddy hurt Mommy.” The couple told investigators they didn’t believe any money had been stolen from the house, because Lewis “never left that kind of money around the house for any reason,” according to the police report. They also stated that given the trouble in the relationship, if Snookie “knew the money was in the house she would have taken it and left him.” At the time of Snookie’s death, Lewis was also involved with a woman named Gail Bloodsaw, according to the police report. When she spoke to police in 1975, she told them she had been going out with Lewis since November 1974. The report notes that Gail said Lewis called her three times between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. on the evening of May 23, 1975. She assumed he was at work because of the machine noise in the background. She also told them he had visited her after work at approximately 12:30 a.m. — around the same time Lewis had placed a call from Kron Street. The police report includes notes from a later interview with Gail Bloodsaw, as well, who the report now described as Lewis’ common-law wife. When she was re-interviewed in 1977, Gail told reporting officers that she had lied to police in her earlier interview and that Lewis had not visited her that night. As she was being interviewed at the station, Lewis arrived and appeared to be “very upset,” according to the report. “Mr. Evans was advised that the Police were just trying to find out who killed his wife & Mr. Evans stated that he did not want the police to do anything regarding the case,” the report states. While at the station, investigators asked Lewis “if he would be willing to speak with Inv. officers about the incident & he refused,” the report notes. During that same 1977 interview, according to the police report, Gail was asked if she had ever forged Snookie’s name on documents, and she replied that she had forged Snookie’s signature during a hospital visit in March 1975 in order to use her health insurance. The police report states that a handwriting expert from the Physical Crimes Unit then examined samples and determined that Gail had also forged Snookie’s signature on a life insurance policy Lewis took out on himself on May 15, 1975, eight days before Snookie’s death. When informed of the finding, Gail said “she believes she may have forged Norris[’s] name to the policy but does not recall doing so,” the report stated. According to the Rochester Police Department, there was not “sufficient evidence to say with certainty the document was forged.” Dateline reached out by phone to Gail Bloodsaw Evans for comment on the events of 1975. She responded, “We have no input on that,” and ended the call. John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company provided investigators with an explanation of two life insurance policies involving Snookie. Dateline obtained a copy of the letter from the Rochester Police Department. The first policy was one Snookie had taken out on herself in 1971. In 1973, she changed the policy to update it to her married name and changed the beneficiary from her mother to her husband, according to the letter. The second policy was the one Lewis took out on himself on May 15, 1975. The letter stated that policy included “Family Insurance” of $1,250 on each of his children, and $1,000 on his wife. The policy also included “Decreasing Term Insurance on the Insured’s wife in the amount of $10,000 for 25 years.” John Hancock noted Lewis Evans was the beneficiary in the event of the death of his wife. The company, “knowing of no reason why payment should not be made in accordance with the Beneficiary Designation of record, paid the policy proceeds to Mr. Evans,” the letter states. In one of his interviews with police in the days following Snookie’s death, Lewis “denied killing his wife and stated that he spent the entire night, from 3:30PM. to 12:08 AM at work (Roch. Prod.)” According to the report, Lewis’ timecard from Rochester Products shows he clocked in at 3:54 p.m. The report also shows that investigators interviewed Lewis’ supervisor who said he relieved Lewis twice on the night of May 23, 1975: during a meal break at 7:55 until about 8:30 or 8:40 p.m., and again from about 10 to 10:30 p.m. Co-workers interviewed by police reported seeing him playing cards at the plant after 11 p.m. The report notes that Lewis’ timecard shows he clocked out at 12:08 a.m. After speaking with witnesses at the plant, “we cannot implicate Evans as being involved in his wifes [sic] death as we can find no-one to say he left the building,” the police report states. Rochester police interviewed two of Lewis’ male relatives: his half brother Leroy Barnes and their cousin Jessie Martin. The three were very close, Ellen said. Neighbors frequently saw them outside Lewis’ home at 5 Kron Street, according to the case report. Leroy and Jessie were at Lewis’ house the afternoon of May 23, 1975, helping him paint his car, they told police at the time. Jessie told police he walked home when Lewis left for work and stayed there the rest of the night. Leroy said he went to the park until about 7:30 p.m., after which he went to a series of bars and nightclubs, which several alibi witnesses confirmed. Both Leroy and Jessie refused polygraph tests, according to the report. The file also details that a neighbor visited Snookie from about 7:15 to 7:30 p.m., around the same time she called Gina to ask if she wanted to play cards. A different neighbor walked by around 7:45 p.m. and saw Snookie sitting on her front porch. That was the last time anyone reported seeing Snookie alive. Two other neighbors were on a nearby porch from about 11:30 p.m. to 12:15 a.m. Other than Officer Camping’s first arrival, neither of them saw anything out of the ordinary at 5 Kron Street, the police report says. Ellen Evans and Gina Alves told Dateline the family was convinced of Lewis’ involvement. “I don’t know if he physically did it, or there was something that was going on that he had a part in,” Gina said. “But the whole family just felt that.” Decades cold When Snookie’s children, Tamara and Daryl, read the contents of the police report in 2021, they saw their mother’s death in a new light. The siblings told Dateline they had remained in their father’s care, and despite rumors in the extended family, were largely kept in the dark about their mom’s case. “I only knew that she was killed, and that it was someone she knew, because there were no signs of forced entry,” Tamara told Dateline. Both Tamara and Daryl can only remember a handful of times Snookie was mentioned as they were growing up. They also say their father kept them away from their mother’s side of the family. “I rarely heard him speak about her personality as a mother, how she nurtured us, cared for us, or what she was like in daily family life after Daryl and I were born,” Tamara wrote in a follow-up email to Dateline. “I wish I had more of those kinds of memories and stories.” “You hear tidbits of information growing up,” Daryl said. But after reading the police report, he says, everything came together. “I really saw a clear picture of who, what, when, why, where.” Tamara and Daryl told Dateline that after reading through the police report, they called on the Rochester Police Department to look into the case again. It was assigned to Investigator Seth Carr of the Major Crimes Unit in 2022. “The truth is, I kid you not, I walked into Capt. Umbrino’s office, and I told him this case should be on Dateline,” Investigator Carr said. “The kids being involved in trying to figure out what happened to their mother, even with the understanding that that may result in their father being implicated. You know, it’s an interesting dynamic.” Over the next couple of years, Investigator Carr conducted several follow-up interviews, including with Lewis Evans. According to Carr, Lewis gave the same response to every question: “I have nothing to add and nothing to take away.” Carr says he’s considered whether the timing of the 11:24 p.m. anonymous phone call to police could have been intended to steer investigators toward a period when certain people in the case had stronger alibis. “There’s certainly a possibility that that’s not a coincidence,” he said. “That this phone call is made and their alibis are strongest at that time, because maybe the goal is to make the police department believe that the crime occurred at that time.” Considering a time-of-death window wider than the estimated 11:30 p.m. to 12:30 a.m. period opens up new potential scenarios, he added. No one has been charged in connection with the case, and no suspects have been named in Snookie’s death. “It’s fair to say Jessie Martin, Lewis Ev[a]ns and Leroy Barnes (deceased) all remain persons of interest in the case,” Carr said in a follow-up email. When Dateline contacted Lewis Evans about Snookie’s case, he responded: “I don’t know anything about that. Have a good day.” He has declined further calls. Dateline also attempted to contact Jessie Martin for comment. His wife answered the phone and said he was unavailable to speak with us. Dateline asked her to pass along our message, but we have not heard back. The way forward Regarding the case status, Rochester Police Capt. Frank Umbrino and Investigator Carr agree: someone must come forward for the case to progress. Although several forensic samples were pulled from the crime scene — including hair, blood, and fabric — they were not preserved properly to undergo modern forensic testing, Capt. Umbrino told Dateline. “We would need somebody that has direct knowledge of who did the murder, who orchestrated the murder, and they would have to be willing to get up on a stand and testify,” he said. “That’s the only thing that’s going to push this case forward.” Ellen Evans has lived 51 years without her sister. The grief never left. “For years I’d cry,” Ellen said. “Her young life was cut short. She had so much to give.” Tamara Sinclair has lived all but three months of her life without her mother. She says she wakes up every day and thinks about her. She wishes she could call her and tell her about her own children. When asked what justice might look like, Tamara wasn’t sure. “I would have accepted accountability and an apology,” she said. “If the truth could just come out,” Gina Alves said. “I just think that one way or another, you just can’t get away with things.” There is one positive outcome to the siblings’ search for answers. Back in 2021, Gina stumbled across Tamara’s Facebook post asking if anyone knew what happened to her mother. She and Snookie’s cousin separated decades ago, and she hadn’t seen Tamara and Daryl since they were children. After seeing the post, they reconnected. “All these years I’m wondering what happened to Snookie’s babies,” she said. “And then I actually got to see Tiger and I got to see Tammy, and all I could do was just hug them and hug them and hug them.” “I always felt that Snookie was their guardian angel,” she said. “She watched over her babies all these years.” If you have information about the Norris “Snookie” Evans case, you can submit a tip to Rochester NY Unsolved or call the Rochester Police Department’s Major Crimes Unit at 585-428-7157. To leave a tip anonymously, please call Rochester Area Crime Stoppers at 585-423-9300. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Mexican governor facing US drug charges seeks leave just one day after returning to office
articles.summary: Embattled Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya's abrupt reversal follows pointed remarks from Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum about putting nation above personal interest.
articles.body: Embattled Sinaloa, Mexico, Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya abruptly requested an indefinite leave of absence Saturday, just one day after returning to office following a three-month absence triggered by U.S. drug trafficking charges against him. Rocha, 77, shared a letter on social media asking for "temporary leave of an indefinite nature, for more than 30 days" from his position as governor. The letter, dated Aug. 22 and stamped received by the Sinaloa State Congress that day, does not say when Rocha plans to return or why he is stepping away again. MEXICAN SENATOR ACCUSES SHEINBAUM OF SHIELDING 'NARCO-POLITICIANS' AFTER US CARTEL INDICTMENT The request came just a day after Rocha announced his return and said it was his "duty to fulfill the mandate" of voters who elected him to serve through Oct. 31, 2027. "Today, I return to the exercise of my responsibility as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience and head held high, with the strength of truth on our side," Rocha wrote Friday on X. Rocha said he spent 112 days away from office while making himself available to Mexican authorities investigating what he called "false accusations" by the U.S. government. He said he personally appeared before Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office and answered investigators’ questions. Rocha insisted the investigation had produced no evidence that he committed a crime and accused political opponents in Mexico and abroad of trying to damage both the country’s sovereignty and the left-wing movement he represents. MEXICAN PRESIDENT IN THE DARK ABOUT DRUG OPERATION AFTER WHICH US, MEXICAN OFFICIALS WERE KILLED "I am unrelated to and innocent of the fabrications woven against me," Rocha wrote. Rocha’s return Friday did not get a warm reception from Mexico’s ruling Morena party or the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum. Morena said it had no advance knowledge of Rocha’s decision and distanced itself from the move, according to Reuters. Mexico’s Interior Ministry said returning to office was Rocha’s decision alone and noted that the attorney general’s investigation remained open. 5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS Sheinbaum also posted a pointed message on X. "No personal interest can ever stand above the interests of the people and the Nation," she wrote. "Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the Nation is eternal," Sheinbaum added. U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses. The current and former high-ranking government and law enforcement officials are alleged to have partnered with the Sinaloa cartel to distribute massive quantities of narcotics to the United States. Rocha is the first sitting Mexican governor to face charges from the U.S., according to Reuters. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The case has strained relations between the U.S. and Mexico. Sheinbaum has called the charges foreign interference, while Mexico says Washington has not provided enough evidence to justify Rocha’s arrest or extradition.

articles.body:
President Donald Trump arrived at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix event in Washington, D.C., on Sunday afternoon, where his motorcade took him on a lap around the racetrack where IndyCar drivers are expected to reach speeds around 180 mph.

The event is part of semiquincentennial celebrations and includes flyovers by various branches of the military. The Qatari-gifted Air Force One also flew alongside fighter jets as Trump’s motorcade took a lap.

Elsewhere, the details of the failed trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada, which sparked tit-for-tat 50 percent tariffs on certain goods between the two countries, are coming to light.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a Saturday evening interview with The New York Times that, before this weekend, officials had offered to reduce existing tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and cars. He added that the U.S. had also offered to completely eliminate a tax on softwood lumber.

“Obviously, we would completely suspend the 50 percent Section 338 tariffs that we were going to apply to 5 percent of Canadian exports,” Greer told the Times, explaining what would have happen had Canada agreed to the other stipulations.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday he planned to match the U.S.’s new 50 percent tariff “dollar for dollar,” though he has not yet elaborated on the details of these policies. Meanwhile, some lawmakers have called for negotiations to resume before Canada’s tariffs takes effect on Sept. 8.

Trump early Sunday morning appeared to address Canada’s threat of retaliatory levies. In a Truth Social post, he accused the U.S.’s northern neighbor of wanting “the benefits of being a State, without being one,” in a nod to his previous comments floating Canada as the 51st state.

articles.title: Landfill collapse in Guinea kills at least 30 people
articles.summary: Heavy rains wash over the site, triggering a landslide that buries several shacks.
articles.body:
A mountainous heap of refuse has collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea’s capital, Conakry, killing at least 30 people, according to a goverment statement.

Six others were also seriously injured after heavy rains in the Bbessia district’s Dar-es-salam neighbourhood triggered a landslide at the landfill around 3 am (15:00 GMT) on Sunday, which buried nearby shacks.

“Significant material and human resources have been deployed to search for any people who may still be buried, to rescue the victims and to recover the bodies,” the government said in the statement.

Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the site of the deadly accident, as excavators took part in a search-and-rescue operation through the collapsed landfill under the gaze of a crowd of onlookers.

Measures have been taken “to ensure medical care for the wounded” and “assistance for those affected by this tragedy”, the government statement said.

The site was designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lieutenant Colonel Balde Mamadou Bailo, sanitation officer for the Military Engineering Battalion.

Lancine Sylla, the head of the Dar-es-Salaam suburb, where the incident occurred, said he feared a high death toll. “We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue,” he told the AFP news agency.

One of Guinea’s main opposition figures, former Prime Minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident “a tragedy that plunges us into dismay”.

“This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the dump had been announced for this Sunday, August 23,” he said on Facebook.

“It is now up to the competent authorities to establish, with full transparency, the circumstances that led to this disaster and to draw all the necessary conclusions,” he added in the statement posted before the release of the death toll.

The government recently has ordered the expulsion of people near the landfill and safety measures around the site because of a fear of collapses.

Guinea is led by General Mamadi Doumbouya, who came to power in a coup in 2021 before being elected president in December 2025.

articles.title: Cafes, shops shut over 'violation of norms': Iran's hijab crackdown returns as women defy veiling rules
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran's long-running debate over mandatory hijab has resurfaced as hardliners push for stricter enforcement, even as the country grapples with the fall.
articles.body: Iran's long-running debate over mandatory hijab has resurfaced as hardliners push for stricter enforcement, even as the country grapples with the fallout of its conflict with the US.During the height of the conflict, women without headscarves were seen at pro-government gatherings and in state media, suggesting that authorities were reluctant to enforce the rules amid more pressing concerns.In recent weeks, however, conservative clerics and politicians have intensified calls for a crackdown on âpublic nudityâ. State media have reported the closure of cafes, restaurants and shops accused of failing to enforce mandatory dress rules.Businesses face action over hijab rulesOn July 19, at least seven cafes and restaurants in Tehran were shut down for allegedly failing to enforce the mandatory hijab, according to human rights group HRANA. The group has also documented social media accounts being blocked over alleged violations of public dress codes, according to CNN.Authorities have used terms including âviolation of normsâ, âviolation of modestyâ and âfailure to observe Islamic decencyâ in such cases. In one case, HRANA said a boutique was closed âdue to unveilingâ.The Tehran Prosecutor's Office has also warned of serious action against alleged âindecencyâ at cafes, restaurants and shops selling clothing considered inappropriate.In South Khorasan province, 10 cafes were closed over alleged violations of âsocial norms and mandatory hijab rulesâ, the Mehr news agency reported, citing the province's chief prosecutor.State media have meanwhile carried repeated calls from religious leaders for women to observe the hijab, describing it as part of Iran's cultural identity.Women continue to defy rulesThe renewed push comes nearly four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in police custody sparked the nationwide âWoman Life Freedomâ protest movement. Amini had been detained over allegations that she was improperly dressed. The protests were violently suppressed, but widespread defiance of compulsory hijab rules has continued, particularly among young women.There have been several high-profile cases. In June, Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team were sentenced in Qom to 74 lashes and banned from leaving the country for two years. Ahmadi had appeared with uncovered hair and bare shoulders during a livestreamed performance in 2024.Women have also increasingly appeared without headscarves in public and on social media. Videos showing groups of women riding motorcycles without hijabs have circulated online, including footage from Tehran, Shiraz and Isfahan.One Instagram post by a group of women in Shiraz said, âWeâre the motorcycle girls of Shiraz! Shiraz girls, letâs go!â Another post showed around 20 female motorcyclists in Isfahan and described it as âthe biggest female motorcycle event in Isfahan.âPezeshkian questions crackdownIranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has questioned whether stricter laws can change people's behaviour, suggesting that authorities should focus on cultural engagement instead.Referring to an interview with a conservative cleric, Pezeshkian said, âThe cleric mentioned hijabâ¦ Well, there are neighborhoods, there are mosques, go and work on it there! Can you really change peopleâs behavior through laws?âHe also referred to disagreements with his daughter over the issue, asking, âDoes it mean I should force her?!â âChanging behavior is a cultural matter; itâs about belief. You canât create belief in people through force,â he added.Former MP Gholamali Jafarzadeh Imanabadi has similarly argued that officials should focus on inflation and people's livelihoods rather than the hijab.Hardliners demand tougher actionHardliners, however, have stepped up pressure on the government to enforce the rules. Kayhan editor Hossein Shariatmadari has described enforcement as both a legal obligation and a religious duty.According to CNN, a member of Iran's parliament, Mohammad-Taqi Naqdali, said, âWe see what the state of nudity and public vice is like in our midstâ¦Israel and America cannot destroy us, but this decay that has plagued our religious culture and is spreading nudity in a disastrous and widespread manner in society will.âIran's Islamic Penal Code criminalises appearing in public without âIslamic hijabâ, although it does not precisely define the term. A tougher law approved in 2024 proposed expanded penalties and surveillance, but its implementation was halted following intervention by the Supreme National Security Council.For now, authorities appear cautious about launching a full-scale street crackdown. A Tehran woman in her 60s told CNN that women were openly wearing clothes such as crop tops and shorts and that headscarves had become rare.âI donât think they can make these girls wear headscarves again. But then again, thatâs also what we thought when the revolution happened. We never thought they would be able to force us to wear them, but in the end, they did,â she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Golden Girls' kitchen comes to life with cheesecake and '80s nostalgia
articles.summary: The Golden Girls Kitchen pop-up in Austin recreates the iconic sitcom's settings and serves cheesecake flights, Cuban sandwiches and meatball subs.
articles.body: The world of "The Golden Girls" is getting a nostalgic revival in Texas, where a pop-up invites fans back into the sitcom’s familiar Miami setting. The Golden Girls Kitchen, running from Aug. 20 through Nov. 8 in Austin, combines recreations of recognizable settings with food tied to the series, including cheesecake flights, Cuban sandwiches, Sal's Sicilian meatball sub and Miami-style cookies, according to event booking platform Bucket Listers. The pop-up taps into the lasting nostalgia surrounding the sitcom, which starred Betty White, Bea Arthur, Rue McClanahan and Estelle Getty as four friends sharing a home in Miami. RETRO PIZZA HUT DRAWS CUSTOMERS FROM HOURS AWAY AS 1980S NOSTALGIA SENDS SALES SOARING The show became known for the friendship among Rose, Dorothy, Blanche and Sophia, along with the group’s conversations around the kitchen table. Food was often part of those moments, particularly cheesecake, which became one of the sitcom's most recognizable traditions. The women frequently gathered around the kitchen table over slices of cheesecake while talking through relationships, family problems, and other ups and downs in their lives. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Austin pop-up nods to that tradition with cheesecake flights, along with other dishes inspired by the show and its Miami setting, according to Bucket Listers. The familiar kitchen is also among the settings recreated for the experience, complete with the recognizable yellow telephone. The concept has previously appeared in cities including New York City, San Diego and Atlanta, among others. Reaction to earlier versions suggests much of the appeal has centered on nostalgia and how closely the details resemble those from the original series. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES One Reddit user who attended the New York City version said "everything was SO realistic," specifically pointing to the kitchen, porch and Rusty Anchor. "Every 20 minutes, the theme song played, and everyone there sang along!!" the user wrote. Another attendee praised the décor but was less enthusiastic about the meal. "We had a blast but the food definitely was not it," the Reddit user wrote, adding that the cheesecake was good despite being partially frozen.
